extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of history (readers of H. G. Wells' Outline of History)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating the political, military, economic, and social factors that the author identifies as causes of the late Republican crisis in Rome (e.g., loss of citizen-army, rise of professional soldiery, finance, corruption, breakdown of representation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of a press (no newspapers)
rubrics_metrics.description: There were no newspapers in republican Rome; the absence of a press is cited as a major deficiency compared to modern political systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text states 'There were no newspapers,[242]' and treats this lack as a structural weakness that limited dissemination of information and contributed to citizen ignorance and the inability of the popular assembly to summarize or express community will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of elementary political education for the masses
rubrics_metrics.description: The plebeians had no general elementary political education; instruction of the masses in civic and political matters was absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wells notes that education 'was the freak of the individual parent, and the privilege of wealth and leisure' and that 'no one proposes to destroy the ignorance complained of.' He treats mass political ignorance as a root cause of weak political solidarity and poor popular judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence/misuse of representative mechanisms in popular assemblies
rubrics_metrics.description: Practically no use of elected representatives in popular assemblies; the popular assemblies were clumsy and easily manipulated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author explains that phrases like 'popular party' mislead unless qualified, because the comitia and assemblies could be 'worked' by manipulation, and that in effect representation did not function as in modern democracies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gerrymandering and manipulation of voting tribes (comitia tributa)
rubrics_metrics.description: Elaborate trickery to enrol or pack new voters into tribes to control tribal votes; the voting-by-tribes system allowed systematic manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: 'Whenever there was a new enfranchisement ... there would be the most elaborate trickery and counter-trickery to enrol the new voters ... into as few or as many of the thirty old “tribes” as possible.' Examples include crowding or scattering new voters to minimize their influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disenfranchisement by distance and organized client groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Although there were many Roman citizens in Italy, effective voting was confined to residents near Rome; voters were organized into clubs (collegia sodalicia) and clients, enabling control by elites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wells notes that with 300,000 to 900,000 citizens, 'in effect the voting of the popular assembly was confined to a few score thousand resident in and near Rome' and that 'they belonged to clubs ... the rising politician ... went first to the usurers and then with the borrowed money to these clubs.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of omens, intimidation and procedural delay to control outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Voting could be delayed by declaring omens unfavourable; intimidatory tactics could be used against voters who came unarmed or armed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'If the outside voters were moved enough by any question to swarm into the city, it was always possible to put off the voting by declaring the omens unfavourable. If they came in unarmed, they could be intimidated; if they brought in arms, then the cry was raised that there was a plot...'

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of straightforward electoral methods leading to violence
rubrics_metrics.description: The absence of simple, fair electoral procedures made popular movements 'entangled and maddened in constitutional intricacies' and often resulted in bloodshed and insurrection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wells argues that 'without a simple and straightforward electoral method, all popular movements in all ages necessarily become entangled and maddened in constitutional intricacies, and almost as necessarily lead to bloodshed.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Displacement of citizen-soldier model by paid/professional soldiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Roman armies changed from levies of free citizens (with voting power linked to military service) to paid, long-term enlistments leading to a professional army.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passages: 'men were enlisted for longer terms and paid... the paid soldier first appeared' and later Marius' reorganization completed the shift so that soldiers' loyalty moved from the state to their commanders who secured pay and plunder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of a professional army: loss of civic solidarity and personal loyalty to leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: As citizen ties weakened, legions developed esprit de corps and loyalty to personal leaders who provided pay and plunder, undermining broader civic allegiance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: 'As that tie fails, the legions discover another in esprit de corps ... They begin to develop a warmer interest in their personal leaders, who secure them pay and plunder.' This is linked to later adventurer generals and civil strife.

rubrics_metrics.name: Money, credit and financialization as destabilizing forces
rubrics_metrics.description: The rise of cash and credit, speculative practices, usury, and a 'money power' (Equestrian order) fundamentally altered social and political life and contributed to inequality and unrest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic disruption from speculative behavior and debt
rubrics_metrics.description: Speculation, borrowing to buy land, hoarding, and price manipulation led to rising inequality, indebtedness, and social discontent among peasants and smallholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'people borrowed to buy, speculation developed... Farmers were giving up corn and cattle, borrowing money, buying slaves' and 'Many patricians were growing poor and irritated and unscrupulous. ... The growing mass of the expropriated was permeated by ... a sense of being inexplicably bested.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Corruption and bribery of officials and commissioners (e.g., Jugurtha)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bribery of commissioners, senators, and generals by foreign rulers or wealthy interests undermined justice and state capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: 'Jugurtha bought over the Commissioners sent out to watch him, the Senators charged with their prosecution, and the generals in command against him.' The proverb 'pecunia non olet' is critiqued—money 'stank' even in Rome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degradation of slavery and public spectacles as moral indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: State-sanctioned cruelties—savage slavery and gladiatorial combats—are evidence of moral decline and civic barbarism compared to later standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wells documents gladiatorial shows: their growth, the use of prisoners and slaves, rituals (pompa, prælusio), the crowd's role in mercy/killing, and observes that 'This organization of murder as a sport and show serves to measure the great gap in moral standards between the Roman community and our own.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Agrarian decline and loss of yeoman backbone
rubrics_metrics.description: The displacement of embattled farmer-citizens (yeomen) through land concentration, slave labor, and commercial agriculture weakened the traditional military and civic foundation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wells discusses Licinian laws, Tiberius Gracchus' attempts to restore the yeoman class, and that 'The great wars had been won... the embattled farmers of Rome had already largely disappeared,' linking land issues to army recruitment and social instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political use of public works, tax farming and courts (Caius Gracchus example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public contracts, tax-farming, and control of courts could be used as instruments of political patronage and enrichment, provoking resentment and conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'He gave the former the newly bequeathed taxes of Asia to farm, and, what is worse, he gave them control of the special courts set up to prevent extortion. He started enormous public works ... and he is accused of making a political use of the contracts.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Insurrection as the effective method of popular expression when institutions fail
rubrics_metrics.description: When formal representative mechanisms are subverted, the people revert to strikes, insurrections and extra-constitutional measures as their primary means of political expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wells: 'The real method of popular expression in Italy in those days was not the comitia tributa, but the strike and insurrection, the righteous and necessary methods of all cheated or suppressed peoples.' He treats this as a predictable outcome of institutional failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rise of insurrectionary leaders and adventurer generals
rubrics_metrics.description: The political vacuum and social discontent produce ambitious military leaders who mobilize popular grievances for personal power (e.g., Marius, Sulla), destabilizing republican order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter frames the last century as 'a history of insurrectionary leaders and counter-revolutionary leaders' and describes how Marius raised troops from the poor, secured repeated consulships, and inadvertently created personal-army loyalties.
